Summary: The paper builds a controlled comparison of generation strategies for drafting OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited (100 entries with 2-12 references; 515 papers, 96 readable in full via open access, 345 abstract-only, 74 title-only). One model (Claude Opus 5.5) writes, extracts, audits and judges under shared guards, one claim-level audit with one repair round and one scoring procedure; only the strategy varies: direct reading of all papers in one prompt, an agentic curator, an evidence graph, case table first, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, three add-ons, and four 'reading better' variants of direct reading evaluated on 41 held-out entries. The primary endpoint is coverage of 6,652 atomic facts split once, blind to drafts, from OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant text as deposited in ClinVar, credited only in draft text that cites the fact's paper. Main results: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers direct reading's coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries; +43.7 points, +38.3 to +49.1; 45 better, 0 worse, 1 tied; Table 23); at the main settings the agent and the evidence graph are not distinguishable from direct reading (-0.6, -0.5) and case table first trails by 1.9 points (suggestive; Table 1); in a matched ablation on 38 entries the evidence graph leads by 1.8 points (Table 1 bottom); a completeness pass adds 2.6 points on 38 held-out entries with no fall in audit-judged fidelity on 20 audited entries (Tables 29, 32), a gain that over all 41 entries depends on keeping the unrevised draft when the revision is stopped (Table 31); a planted-error test shows the audit catches citation swaps, moved variant sentences and single-value substitutions but not added citations or omissions (Fig. 4, Tables 49-50). No person validated any judgement. All three reviewers rate the paper 5 (Reject, confidence 4). They agree that the design is clean, the access manipulation is convincing, and the statistical reporting and disclosure are well above the norm. They also agree that the claims resting on 0.5-3 point differences are not yet supported: every judgement comes from the writer's own model family with no human validation, the matched-ablation lead is largely an entry-set effect, the recall-only endpoint has no length or precision control, safety-filter stops select entries differently per strategy, and the regime (few references, one long-context model) is the one where strategies are least expected to differ.
Strengths: Clean controlled design: the source set is fixed to the curators' reference list, one model performs every role, and guards (ontology identifiers only from search candidates, HGNC normalisation, removal of recalled cross-references, mandatory citation of a supplied paper), audit and scoring are shared, so the strategy is the only manipulated variable in the main comparison (Sec. 3, Fig. 1, Table 4). This contrasts usefully with prior work that compares designs across tasks, models and scorers (Sec. 2). Fact lists are split once without sight of any draft and reused for every strategy; the earlier per-draft scoring is kept as a row and preserves the ordering (Sec. 3.3, Table 6).

The within-paper access manipulation is the paper's strongest result (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a, Table 23): the same 46 entries and 2,120 fixed facts, with memory and paper identity held constant and no arm repaired, give +43.7 points for full text (95% CI +38.3 to +49.1; 45 better, 0 worse, 1 tied). The effect is large enough that plausible judge error is unlikely to overturn its direction or rough size. The second-hand-passage arm (+4.9 points, +2.8 to +7.1) quantifies a realistic partial substitute.

Statistical reporting is careful and appropriately modest: paired bootstrap intervals over entries, better/worse/tied counts with exact sign tests (the reported p-values check out, e.g. 31/48 gives 0.071, 31/42 gives 0.242, 33/45 gives 0.213), Holm adjustment for secondary measures (Table 8), an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 11), a symmetric completion rule, three replicates and three judgings on 30 entries used as a noise yardstick rather than a test (App. E, Table 20), and an explicit refusal to claim equivalence without a pre-set margin (Sec. 4.2). Every analysis is labelled primary, secondary, post hoc or exploratory (Sec. 3.3, Tables 2-3).

The stated/not-stated decomposition (Fig. 2b-c, Fig. 3, Table 19) makes the headroom explicit: reading strategies convey 91.0-94.4% of facts the supplied text states and 5.5-6.9% of facts it does not, no better than the memory-only control (8.2%). This explains why designs separate by only a few points in this regime, and the completeness pass then recovers gains where the decomposition predicts (+4.5 points on stated full-text facts, no change on unstated facts; Fig. 3b, Table 29).

The reading-better experiment follows good practice for its first three arms: prompts written on three training entries and frozen before the 41 held-out entries ran, Holm adjustment across arms, fidelity audited on 20 entries (Table 32), and the dependence of the completeness-pass gain on the stopped-revision rule reported in the main text (Sec. 4.3, Table 31) rather than hidden.

The audit stress test gives a concrete, transferable finding for cited-generation systems: the best-verdict-over-cited-papers rule hides over-citation (0 of 30 added citations flagged although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for 176 of 176 claims; Table 49), zygosity and single-family deletions go undetected (0/8, 0/2; Table 50), and 4-7% of (claim, cited paper) pairs in real multi-citation paragraphs are not supporting (Table 52). The unaltered re-audit control (0/60 and 0/113 flagged) is a sensible addition.

Memory and contamination are handled seriously: a memory-only control by creation era (Fig. 5, Table 16), 20 compared entries created in 2026 that were not used in development and whose stored drafts are reproduced exactly (App. M.2), where memory-only coverage falls to 7.0% and memory gene F1 to 30.0% while direct reading conveys 52.2%, and a provenance analysis of conveyed facts (Table 18).

Reporting is unusually candid: deviations from design, the earlier analysis that had put the evidence graph 2.1 points behind direct reading before completion became symmetric (App. M.4), every dropped entry by ID (Tables 5, 28, 54), every safety-filter stop, cost per strategy and in total (Table 12; about $3,587), and release of per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores.
Weaknesses: No judgement is validated by a person, and one model family splits the reference, marks facts present/partly/absent/contradicted, decides what the supplied text 'states' and audits (Sec. 3.3; Limitations i-ii). The only reliability evidence is self-consistency (95.7% per-fact agreement between two judgings; App. E, Table 20), and App. M.3, where the judge sided with the draft against the reference in 22 of 37 contradictions, shows judge-reference disagreements are unresolved. The access effect survives this, but the strategy differences (-1.9 to +1.8 points) and the reading-better gains (+1.6 to +3.3) are the size a modest, strategy-dependent judge bias (self-preference, cited in Sec. 2, or differential crediting of paraphrase versus extracted quotes) could create or erase. The stated/not-stated analyses (Fig. 2b-c, Fig. 3, Table 19) add a structural correlation: a fact the model cannot quote from the text is plausibly also one it fails to convey, which Sec. 4.1 concedes holds 'partly by construction', so the 4% headroom and the 91.0-94.4% coverage of stated facts inherit it. All three reviewers consider an expert-labelled stratified sample with chance-corrected agreement and per-strategy error rates (or at least a second judge family on a subset) necessary before the small-difference claims can be relied on.

The matched-ablation headline is mainly an entry-set effect, yet the abstract, Introduction and Sec. 4.2 present it as a settings effect ('with settings matched, the evidence graph leads by 1.8 points'; 'the order of close designs depends on settings'). App. F and Table 22 show that on the same 38 entries the main-settings evidence graph is already +1.0 (-0.9 to +2.8; drafts identical to the main run), the settings change itself is +0.8 (-0.5 to +2.1; 18/12), and the graph's sign differs between the 19 ablation entries with half or more full text (-1.2) and the other 19 (+3.1). App. E likewise attributes the graph's lead on the 30-entry replicate subset versus -0.5 on the 93 main entries to which entries are averaged. The 38 entries are a non-random subset weighted towards full text, chosen after the main comparison, with no multiplicity adjustment. Only the case table's matched gain (+2.1, +1.1 to +3.2) directly supports dependence on settings.

The primary endpoint is recall-only with no length or precision counterpart. Drafts make about twice as many statements per paper as the reference has facts and only about 24% of statements have a counterpart (App. H). The reading-better arms lengthen drafts from 10,802 characters to 11,837, 14,412 and 14,245 (Table 33), roughly in step with their gains (+1.6, +2.6, +3.1), and the extract-then-write drafts carry 12-17% more audited claims per entry (Table 6: 113.5 and 117.9 vs 101.0). The audit checks fidelity, not relevance, so the gains cannot yet be attributed to the completeness mechanism rather than to writing more. Separately, variant precision counts a variant OMIM does not list as a miss even when the paper reports it (Sec. 3.3, Table 10), which conflates errors with legitimate extras and penalises the extract-first designs.

The regime and the single writer model limit the strategy conclusion. Entries have 2-12 references that fit one prompt, 81% of papers are abstract- or title-only, and 2,669 of 6,239 compared facts are stated in no supplied text (Sec. 5, Table 19); Sec. 5 concedes this regime favours direct reading. The settings that motivate agentic and extract-first designs were attempted but yielded no comparison: 0 of 4 large entries (76-148 references) were completed by every strategy (App. K.2), the 30-75-reference tier is reported without findings (App. M.1), and no second or smaller-context writer was run (Limitation ii). 'Strategy matters little' is thus established only where it is most expected, and the title and abstract ('Strategy or access?') read as more general than the evidence.

The reference is indirect and variant-centred, which bounds both the access effect and what the endpoint can see. The task is a phenotype entry, but scoring uses OMIM allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar, credited only in text citing that paper (Sec. 3.1; Limitation iv). Fig. 2b shows the supplied text states about 76% of facts about full-text papers but 26% of those about abstract-only papers, so the 43.7-point magnitude is a property of this reference as much as of reading; the access effect on the independently curated HPO-synopsis reference is not reported for the hidden-full-text experiment (Table 23). The main text does not say how many of the 515 papers have an in-scope paragraph or what share of each draft cites them, and for large entries only 5-10% of references are scored (Table 48). Most draft content is therefore checked only by the same-model audit, whose sensitivity estimates rest on 2-8 items per qualifier rule (Fig. 4, Table 50).

Safety-filter stops act as an uncontrolled, strategy-dependent selection mechanism. Completion differs by arm: 7 of 100 entries are dropped from the main comparison (Table 5), the completeness arms lose 3 and 6 of 41 entries (Table 28), 10 of 30 entries created in 2026 are dropped and the agentic curator alone loses 6 (Table 54), the large-entry tier loses all 4 and STORM completes nothing (App. J, K.2). The same three entries (118210, 617232, 621030) lose a paper in the evidence graph (Table 5) and lose the whole draft in both completeness arms (Table 28), consistent with content-dependent stops. Counting a lost entry as zero turns the completeness gains of +2.4 and +3.1 into -3.5 and -4.8 (Table 31), so the reported gain depends on a fallback rule the harness adopted after the evaluation (Sec. 4.3; Reproducibility statement). No analysis checks whether stopped entries differ in topic, size, access or era (Limitation ii).

Analytic flexibility is high relative to the effect sizes. Fixed fact lists replaced per-draft splitting; completion became symmetric after a first analysis put the evidence graph 2.1 points behind (Sec. 3.3, App. M.4); the matched ablation ran after the main comparison; the stated/not-stated restrictions, the no-repair rescoring and the stopped-revision sensitivity analysis are post hoc; the claim-selection rule for deleted qualifiers was widened after the run, recovering two flagged negation items (App. L); and the combined 'checklist with completeness pass' arm was designed after the other three arms' held-out results were seen and is then compared with the baseline as primary on the same held-out entries (Sec. 4.3, App. I), which sits uneasily with Sec. 3.3's statement that reading-better prompts were frozen before the held-out entries ran. The primary endpoint is unadjusted across five comparisons, and the main strategies were developed on their evaluation entries (Limitation viii), with only 20 entries created in 2026 held out. Each change is disclosed and several are improvements, but together they make the 1-2 point ordering claims exploratory in practice.

Contribution (1), a reusable benchmark, is weaker than claimed. The fixed fact lists contain curator wording and are not redistributed (Sec. 3.1 'Reuse'; Ethics statement), so a rebuilt reference must be split again; the stability of a fresh split by the same procedure was not measured, and a different splitting procedure moved levels by 2-5 points (Table 6). The interface exposes no temperature or seed, and the model's safety filter decides completion. Third parties therefore cannot score a new strategy on the reported denominators; the work is better described as a controlled study with released drafts and scores.

Non-inferiority claims lack margins or intervals. The abstract's 'without lowering the share of claims judged supported' rests on 20 of the 38 compared entries (97.2% vs 97.0%; Table 32) with no interval or pre-set margin, and the abstract's 'not distinguishable from reading all papers in one prompt' reads more strongly than Sec. 4.2's careful 'this is not an equivalence claim'.

The released-pipeline comparison (Sec. 4.4, App. J) is too limited for main-text space: PaperQA2 ran without its agent on 10 entries, GraphRAG on 4 and STORM on none (every research-stage prompt stopped), under a different protocol (six section questions concatenated rather than a written entry) and with a substituted small embedder. The -14.5-point PaperQA2 gap mixes design with protocol, as Limitation xi concedes.

Clarity suffers from density and coined terminology. Most main-text sentences carry several estimates, intervals and caveats; the reader must track repaired/unrepaired, like for like, completes, stated, pooled vs mean over entries, fixed vs per-draft scoring, and the 93/46/41/38/35/20-entry sets; key definitions are compressed into one paragraph of Sec. 3.3; Sec. 4.4 compresses four experiments into one paragraph; and the paper runs to 53 pages with 54 tables. Several small internal inconsistencies are listed in the next item. The title does not tell an ML reader what the task is.

Internal inconsistencies and gaps in the text: (i) Sec. 4.1 hides 'the 91 papers readable in full' in 49 entries (also Table 2), whereas Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 1 count 96 full-text papers, and the other 5 are not accounted for; (ii) Sec. 4.5 lists deleted negations among 'six further classes of 30 items each' that were 'all caught', whereas negation is an 8-item rule inside the 30-item deleted-qualifier class (Fig. 4, Table 50), and two of the 8 catches come from the claim-selection rule widened after the run (App. L); (iii) Table 1's matched block gives variant precision for the case table (76.5) but '-' for the evidence graph without explanation, and App. F lists precision for the main-settings and plus-text graph (81.4, 84.4) but not for the matched graph; (iv) App. F and Table 22 give different intervals for the same estimates (graph +1.0: -0.8 to +2.9 vs -0.9 to +2.8; case table -2.3: upper bound +0.0 vs +0.1), which App. F attributes to a separate bootstrap but which leads readers to quote different numbers. Methodological novelty for the ICLR audience is also modest: no new method is proposed (Sec. 2 says so) and the measurement lessons of Sec. 5 are largely established good practice.
Questions: Can you add expert labels on a stratified sample (for example 300-500 facts across strategies, access levels and stated/not-stated classes, plus a sample of audit verdicts) and report chance-corrected agreement with the model judge? Do judge error rates differ between direct-reading and extract-then-write drafts, and do the main strategy differences and the stated/not-stated contrast survive on expert labels? Could a judge from a second model family re-judge a subset to estimate self-preference and correlated errors between 'stated' and 'conveyed'?

Given that the main-settings evidence graph is already +1.0 on the 38 ablation entries and the matched-minus-main change is +0.8 (-0.5 to +2.1) (Table 22, App. F), will you revise the abstract, Introduction and Sec. 4.2 to attribute the graph's lead mainly to entry selection, and restate 'the order of close designs depends on settings' accordingly? Was the 38/40-entry subset fixed before per-entry main-comparison results were seen?

Can you report a length-controlled view of the primary endpoint for each strategy and reading-better arm (coverage per 1,000 characters, or the share of per-paper statements with a reference counterpart), or add a length-matched direct-reading control (e.g., told to be exhaustive per paper at about 14,000 characters)? Of the variants the extract-first designs generate that OMIM does not list (Table 10), how many are reported in the cited papers?

Do safety-filter stops cluster by paper, topic, number or length of papers, access level or creation era? Please characterise the lost entries (e.g., 118210, 617232, 621030) and report best- and worst-case bounds, or imputation by the entry's direct-reading score, for the main comparison, the reading-better arms and the 2026 entries.

Could a second writer family, especially a smaller-context model for which extract-first designs are motivated, be run on the 30 replicate or 38 ablation entries? Is there any setting (entries above the single-prompt budget with a writer that is not stopped) in which the strategies can be compared where they are expected to differ?

Why does the hidden-full-text experiment hide 91 papers in 49 entries when 96 of the 515 papers are readable in full? What is the effect of hiding full text on the HPO-synopsis measures, whose reference is largely curated independently of OMIM's variant text?
How many of the 515 cited papers have at least one in-scope curator paragraph, and what share of each draft's text cites such papers?

How much do levels and paired differences move under a fresh split by the same procedure (e.g., re-splitting 20-50 entries)? Could you release fact identifiers with hashed content, or a scoring service, so others can score against your denominators without redistributing curator text?

Would you report a post hoc equivalence test (e.g., TOST at +/-2 points) for the agentic curator and the evidence graph against direct reading, and an interval or pre-specified non-inferiority margin for the completeness pass's share of claims judged supported, ideally auditing all 38 compared entries rather than 20?
How sensitive are the paired differences, not only the levels, to the half-credit for 'partly present'? Table 6 reports full-credit-only levels but not full-credit-only differences or intervals.

Using the per-paper verdicts recovered for 80-88% of entries (Table 52), how many real paragraphs would an 'any cited paper fails' rule flag, and how many are genuine over-citations on manual inspection? Did you consider a qualifier-specific check, given that deleted zygosity and 'one family' qualifiers were not caught (0/8, 0/2; Table 50)?

What explains the oldest band's much lower direct-reading coverage (34.9% against 51.2-53.9%; Table 16), and how much of abstract-only coverage comes from inference or recall, given that 34.2% of facts conveyed from abstract-only papers are only partly stated and 4.1% are in no supplied text (Table 18)?
Limitations: The authors' limitations section (Sec. 5, i-xi) is thorough and candid: no human validation, one model family, no comparable results on large sets of papers, an indirect reference, the reference list given to every strategy, open-access text only without supplements, development on the evaluation entries, single runs, and the audit's blind spots.

Not adequately addressed: the recall-type primary endpoint has no length control or precision counterpart, which affects how the reading-better gains and the merge result should be read (Table 33; App. H).

Not stated plainly enough: the ordering of close strategies depends on which entries are averaged (App. E: graph ahead on the 30-entry subset in all replicates, behind on the 93; App. F: graph +1.0 on the 38 ablation entries at main settings), not only on settings; the abstract should reflect this.
The magnitude of the access effect is specific to a variant-centred reference whose facts live mostly in full text, and should be presented as conditional on this reference.

The single model's safety filter determines which entries and systems can be compared (main set, reading-better arms, 2026 entries, large entries, STORM), and the reading-better gain depends on a fallback rule adopted after the evaluation (Table 31; Reproducibility statement).

The curator-derived fact lists cannot be redistributed and the stability of a fresh split is unmeasured, so third parties cannot reproduce scores on the same denominators (Sec. 3.1; Ethics statement).

Generated drafts concern human genetic disease. The Ethics statement appropriately requires that they be marked as machine generated and not presented as OMIM content or clinical guidance; the audit's blindness to deleted zygosity, hedges, over-citation and omissions should be stated prominently in any released harness, since a passed audit certifies neither correctness nor completeness.
